title: Instagram Modernized its UI with an AI-Native Architecture, Cutting Token Costs by 33%
gist: Instagram Direct migrated its Android UI from the legacy View system to Jetpack Compose with an explicitly AI-native architecture, reporting 50% less UI code, 33% lower token cost per agent session and 35% faster agent execution. The key lesson is to design architecture so the agent's path of least resistance yields correct code.

insights.claim: Instagram Direct's migration of its Android UI from the legacy View system to Jetpack Compose reduced UI code volume by 50%, AI agent execution time by 35%, token costs per agent session by 33% and engineer-agent exchanges by 32%.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: A concrete example of codebase design lowering AI coding costs; token spend per session is a measurable lever.

insights.claim: Instagram engineers argue the right unit of AI migration is the underlying architecture, not prompting agents to migrate individual components piecemeal.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Suggests AI-readiness assessments should evaluate architecture, not just tool adoption.
insights.locator: Rather than taking a piecemeal approach

insights.claim: AI coding agents take the path of least resistance, so unguided they tend to introduce subtle bugs, tech debt and performance regressions; the design should make the correct path the easiest and poor decisions hard and expensive to express.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Codebase guardrails and architectural boundaries become a quality lever as agent-written code grows.
insights.quote: AI agents naturally take the path of least resistance, so the design should make that path lead to correct, high-quality code, while making poor design decisions hard and expensive to express.

insights.claim: Minimizing context dependency means favoring established best practices and familiar patterns over codebase-specific knowledge, which helps agents produce more reliable results.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Conventional frameworks are easier for models to work with than bespoke internal ones.
insights.locator: Another key principle is minimizing context dependency

insights.claim: Instagram standardized AI-assisted workflows across the team to keep consistency with shared architectural conventions, and carried out the migration without stopping engineers from shipping features.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Shows large AI-assisted migrations can run alongside product work.

insights.claim: The team tracked three production metrics at runtime: time to interact, time to fully load and scroll performance, enabling A/B tests of the Compose UI against the legacy UI.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Runtime production metrics with A/B testing are the gating evidence for risky UI rewrites.

insights.claim: Performance could not be assessed reliably until entire screens were ported to Compose, because remaining legacy Views distorted measurements.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Partial migrations give misleading benchmarks; plan whole-screen cutovers.

insights.claim: Compose components had to be compatible with both RecyclerView and LazyColumn and switchable at runtime via feature flags for A/B testing; the team eventually replaced RecyclerView with LazyColumn.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Feature-flagged dual-path design is what made the migration measurable and reversible.

insights.claim: Compose has a runtime warmup cost incurred only once per app session, so migrating additional screens improved startup performance elsewhere in the app.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Gains compound as more screens move to Compose.
